title: Covariate-Conditional Scaling of Residual Dispersion Shortens Detection Delay in Patient-Based Real-Time Quality Control Without Splitting Patients
content: Background/Objectives: In patient-based real-time quality control (PBRTQC), covariate adjustment targets the mean of the residual, while dispersion is handled by a global transformation or by splitting patients into groups, at the cost of sample size. Whether dispersion can be modelled continuously as a function of the same covariates, and whether this shortens detection, is unknown. Methods: We analysed 1,258,547 consecutive biochemistry results (18 analytes, 288 days, one analyser). Residuals came from Box-Cox transformation and covariate regression; the arms differed only in the denominator, a single standard deviation or a conditional scale from quantile regression. Both used the same exponentially weighted moving average and decision rule, were calibrated to 0.1% false alarm, and were compared over 40 injected shifts of 1×TEa. The comparison was repeated with shared exponent and window. External validation used 2023 data with reagents from different suppliers. Results: Detection was faster in 13 of 18 analytes (12–66%; geometric mean ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.59–0.87; exploratory P = 0.004), with no analyte excluded. Under shared parameters the gain persisted in creatinine (0.36), albumin (0.64) and total protein (0.39), was halved in triglyceride (0.82), disappeared in calcium (1.06) and reversed in glucose (1.98; 276 versus 1248 samples at exponents of −1.5 and +2.0). Below 0.6–0.7×TEa the conditional arm was slower. Conclusions: Modelling dispersion continuously shortens detection in a subset of analytes without splitting patients, and the gain is not an artefact of per-arm tuning. It appears only above about 0.7×TEa, so comparisons should report matched-parameter results alongside optimised ones.
